title: Ultrasonic Testing for Fabrication Shops | UT Welds (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic weld inspection for US fabricators: AWS D1.1 structural steel, ASME Section VIII vessels, B31.3 spools, API 650 tanks. Request a UT quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Fabrication and Welding Shops in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing (UT) of welds, plate and shop-fabricated components for fabricators and their owners across the United States: structural steel, pressure vessels, piping spools and storage tank shells. Technicians are mobilized to the fabricator's shop or yard, examine to the governing code, and report indications with location, size and accept or reject status. To scope a job, request a UT inspection quote with your weld map and code.

What UT does in a fabrication shop

Fabrication is where most weld defects are either caught or shipped. A fabricator makes thousands of joints a month, each welded by a qualified welder to a qualified procedure, and then a share of them is examined before the work is painted, hydrotested or loaded onto a truck. Ultrasonic testing is the volumetric method in that mix: sound energy travels through the full thickness of the joint, so it reports on lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, slag and cracking that a surface method cannot see. Our ultrasonic weld inspection page covers the technique itself; this page covers how it fits the fabrication floor.

Typical shop scopes include complete joint penetration groove welds in building and bridge-type structural steel, longitudinal and circumferential seams on carbon steel and low-alloy pressure vessels, butt welds on process piping spools, and shell-to-shell and shell-to-annular joints on field-erected and shop-built tanks. UT is also used on rolled plate before welding to look for laminations that would interfere with an angle-beam examination or with a nozzle or lug weld later.

Codes that drive the examination

The examination is never a matter of preference. The contract names a code, the code names a method and a percentage, and the acceptance criteria belong to that code. The documents we work to most often in fabrication are:

  • AWS D1.1, Structural Welding Code - Steel, for buildings and general structures. Its ultrasonic provisions set the equipment, calibration, scanning and acceptance rules for groove welds, and they apply an indication rating system rather than a flat size limit.
  • ASME Section VIII, Divisions 1 and 2, for shop-built pressure vessels, with examination methods taken from ASME Section V and the written procedure qualified against the code's demonstration requirements.
  • ASME B31.3 for process piping spools, where the number of welds examined depends on the fluid service category.
  • API 650 for welded tanks, where the standard decides which seams must be examined and by which method.

The explanation of the examination article itself is in our guide to ASME Section V Article 4 ultrasonic requirements. Acceptance is decided by the code, applied by the owner's inspector, the fabricator's quality manager or a third party named in the contract, never by the technician alone. We report; the party named in the contract accepts.

Fabricator QC, owner QA, and where we fit

Fabrication quality sits on two sides of a fence. The fabricator runs quality control: welder and procedure qualifications, fit-up checks, in-process visual examination, and the NDT its own quality plan requires. The owner, or an engineering firm acting for the owner, runs quality assurance: audits, surveillance, and the witness or review of selected examinations. Hold points are the places in the plan where work stops until someone has looked, such as after root pass, after fit-up, or after final weld and before post-weld heat treatment.

We are engaged by either side. A fabricator without full-time UT capacity uses us to examine to its own quality plan. An owner or contractor uses us to audit a sample of the fabricator's work independently. The role is different and so is the report, so tell us which one applies when you request a quote. Where the contract requires a customer-witnessed examination, we schedule the examination to the hold point and the witness sees the calibration, the scan and the evaluation, not just the paper.

What UT finds in fabricated welds, and what it misses

On a groove weld in plate, shear wave UT is strong on planar flaws oriented across the beam: lack of sidewall fusion, lack of root fusion, cracks and incomplete penetration. It is weaker on porosity and small, rounded slag, which reflect little energy and are rated more easily by other means. It also depends on access: the transducer must reach the sound path from the base metal beside the weld, so a joint with a pad, a stiffener or a tight corner may need a different beam angle or a different approach.

Method choice is part of our job. Surface cracks at weld toes and in heat-affected zones on carbon steel are found efficiently by magnetic particle inspection of fabricated welds, and open-to-the-surface flaws on stainless steel and aluminum are the territory of liquid penetrant testing in fabrication. Many fabrication scopes combine two of the three; our weld inspection page explains how they are sequenced.

Technique details that decide whether the examination is valid

A valid ultrasonic examination starts before the transducer touches the plate. The flaw detector is calibrated on a block of the same acoustic material as the weldment, to the range and sensitivity the procedure sets, and the calibration is checked again at the intervals the procedure names and whenever the setup changes. The technician selects the beam angle to suit the thickness and the weld bevel, marks the scan area on the surface, and cleans away spatter, scale and loose paint so the couplant film is continuous.

  • Surface condition: a rough or shot-blasted surface needs a heavier couplant; a ground surface needs less. We note surface condition on the report because it affects sensitivity.
  • Scanning pattern: the transducer is moved side to side as it approaches the weld, covering the whole volume of the weld and heat-affected zone from the faces the procedure requires.
  • Temperature: preheated or freshly welded material changes sound velocity and can damage couplant; the procedure sets a temperature window and we scan outside it only with a qualified adjustment.
  • Thickness and geometry: thin material limits the useful angle and the number of skips; thick sections may need additional angles to reach the root.

Section VIII shop vessels and the radiography question

Pressure vessel work raises a question we hear regularly: can UT replace radiography on a full-radiography vessel? ASME Section VIII allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under defined conditions, and those conditions call for computerized imaging techniques that Atlantis does not offer on these pages. For code-required radiography, the owner or fabricator must use a licensed radiography contractor. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under federal and state rules.

What we do for the vessel shop is the work that Section VIII and Section V assign to conventional UT and surface methods: examination of nozzle and attachment welds where the code allows it, plate and forging examination to the purchase specification, and checks that supplement a radiography program. For the broader shop vessel context see our pressure vessel inspection services page.

What the UT report contains

A fabrication report is a record that outlives the job, so it has to stand on its own years later. Ours is built around the items an auditor, an owner or a code inspector asks for first.

UT report contents for a fabrication scope
ItemWhat it records
IdentificationJob, drawing and weld number, joint type, material, thickness and welder or procedure reference where supplied
ProcedureWritten procedure number and revision, code edition and the acceptance standard applied
EquipmentFlaw detector, transducer type, frequency and angle, calibration block and couplant, with the calibration check results
PersonnelTechnician name and qualification level under the written practice, and the Level III who approved the procedure
ResultsEvery recordable indication with location along the weld, depth, length and amplitude relative to the reference level, plus accept or reject
SketchesWeld map with indication positions marked, so repair crews can find them

Rejects are called out in a separate list so the fabricator can plan repair and re-examination; re-examined areas are reported against the original weld number.

What to send us for a quote

A quote is only as accurate as the information behind it. To scope fabrication UT, send:

  • The applicable code and edition, plus any customer specification that tightens it
  • Weld map or joint list with joint types, quantities and the percentage to be examined
  • Material grade and thickness range for each joint type
  • Written procedure, if you have one; if not, we can draft and qualify one with our Level III
  • Hold points, witness requirements and the schedule they drive
  • Access: indoors or outdoors, position of the work, lifts or scaffold, and surface condition
  • Site rules: badging, safety orientation, hot-work or confined-space permits, and the shop address

Planning realities in a fabrication shop

Fabrication shops run on takt time and crane availability. A sound examination plan fits the workflow: weld-out, cool, grind flush where required, examine, then release to the next operation. If UT has to wait for post-weld heat treatment or for painting, the plan has to say so; if the shop welds ahead and examines later, rejects and repair compete with the next job. A UT technician is most productive when the hold points are scheduled with the crane operator and the welding foreman, and when the weld map shows which joints are ready.

We also support welder qualification and procedure qualification work where UT is the method the code names for the test coupon. Where you need a qualified written procedure or a demonstration against the code, our NDT technical procedure development service handles it under Level III review.

Where we work in the United States for fabrication

Our technicians are mobilized to your shop or yard for the agreed scope; there is no Atlantis facility to drop parts at. These city pages describe the fabrication regions we are asked about most for UT:

  • Houston: vessel, skid and piping fabricators along the Gulf Coast corridor.
  • Tulsa: tank, vessel and pipeline equipment fabrication in northeast Oklahoma.
  • Pittsburgh: structural steel, plate and heavy equipment shops in the Ohio River valley.
  • Chicago: structural and miscellaneous steel fabricators serving Midwest construction.
  • Milwaukee: heavy machinery and mining equipment weldments.
  • Peoria: earthmoving-equipment frames and structures.
  • Cleveland: steel processing and industrial fabrication in the Great Lakes belt.
  • Birmingham: pressure equipment and structural fabricators in the Southeast.
  • Beaumont: refinery and petrochemical piping and vessel shops on the Texas Gulf Coast.
  • Oklahoma City: oilfield equipment and structural fabrication.
  • Joliet: heavy steel and tank fabrication near the Illinois waterway.

Training your own UT technicians

Many fabricators prefer in-house UT for routine work and call us for peak load or independent audit. We support that: UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training prepare your people, and the ultrasonic testing simulator lets them practice calibration and scanning before they work on production welds. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel, so the course is one input to your written practice, not a certificate. For the wider industry context, see NDT training for manufacturing.

What we do not do here

Radiography is not part of what Atlantis does in the United States, and specialist ultrasonic techniques are outside this page. Our crews do not weld, repair or grind, we do not act as the owner's authorized inspector, and we do not decide what a fabricator must examine; the code and the contract do that. We provide examination data and written reports that the responsible party uses to accept, reject or repair. Our technicians are qualified under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II technicians perform and interpret, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification for its own management system. See the national UT page and the ultrasonic testing guide for more.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on a Section VIII pressure vessel?
faq.a: Only under conditions that ASME Section VIII spells out, and those conditions call for computerized imaging techniques that Atlantis does not offer on these pages. For code-required radiography you need a licensed radiography contractor; we do not perform radiography in the United States.

faq.q: Do you travel to our fabrication shop or do we ship parts to you?
faq.a: Our technicians are mobilized to your shop or yard. Atlantis has no facility where parts are dropped off, so the scope, access, surface preparation and site rules are agreed before the crew travels to your site.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the welds you examine?
faq.a: The party named in the contract does: the owner, its inspector or the fabricator's quality manager, using the acceptance criteria of the governing code. Our report lists each indication with its location, size and the criterion applied, so that decision can be made quickly.

faq.q: What do you need to quote UT on a fabrication scope?
faq.a: Send the code and edition, a weld map or joint list with quantities and examination percentage, material and thickness, any written procedure, hold points, access conditions and site rules. Missing items are usually the written procedure and the surface condition.

faq.q: Can you witness-support an owner audit of a fabricator?
faq.a: Yes. An owner or contractor can engage us to examine a sample of the fabricator's welds independently, and we report to the party that engaged us. We will confirm the audit scope and reporting line before work starts, so there is no conflict with the fabricator's own QC.

faq.q: Is UT or MT better for finding cracks in structural welds?
faq.a: Magnetic particle inspection is quicker for surface and near-surface cracks on carbon steel, while UT finds buried planar flaws through the full thickness. Many AWS D1.1 scopes use both, and we will recommend the mix after reading your contract documents.

faq.q: Do you examine plate for laminations before welding?
faq.a: Yes, where the purchase specification or the fabrication plan calls for it. A straight-beam scan finds laminations that could later interfere with an angle-beam weld examination or a nozzle attachment, and the results are reported against the plate specification.

faq.q: Do you provide a written procedure for UT?
faq.a: We can draft one under the review of an ASNT NDT Level III and demonstrate it against the code requirements, or work to your existing procedure. Procedure development is a separate scope so that the revision control is clear in the final report.

faq.q: Are your UT technicians certified by Atlantis?
faq.a: In an SNT-TC-1A program each employer issues its own personnel credentials. Our technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, with Level II performing and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports.
